newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa's health shows improvement.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa's health shows improvement.

text.p: Mother Teresa's health showed some improvement on Friday and doctors were meeting to decide if the 86-year-old nun could withstand an X-ray to see if she needs surgery to clear a blocked artery.
Heart clinic officials said the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize winner chatted with one of her doctors over morning tea.
"Mother Teresa is slightly better than yesterday. She had a peaceful night and a good sleep," said a regular medical bulletin issued by the Birla Heart Research Centre.
"The doctors are meeting in another two hours to decide whether they can perform the angiography during the day."
On Thursday, Mother Teresa got up for the first time in seven days and sat in a chair for 30 minutes, doctors said.
She was admitted to the Woodlands Nursing Home in the eastern Indian city of Calcutta on November 22 and was moved to the Birla clinic last Tuesday for an angiography X-ray test.
The test involves an X-ray and an opaque dye injected into blood vessels to check for any arterial blockage.
Doctors have twice delayed the test, originally planned for last Wednesday, because she was too weak.
They said on Thursday that although Mother Teresa remained in critical condition, her vital signs had stabilised sufficiently to make the test possible.
Mother Teresa, known as the "Saint of the Gutters" for her work with the poor, was fitted with a heart pacemaker in 1989.
She has undergone coronary angiography twice -- in the United States in 1991 and at the Birla centre in 1993.
Each time she also had angioplasty, in which surgeons insert a balloon into an artery and inflate it to unblock the artery.
There were indications that Mother Teresa required further surgery, her cardiologist, Dr A.K. Bardhan, said on Thursday.
"All indications lead to the conclusion that she has a blockage in her coronary artery," Bardhan told Reuters.
"What happened last Friday was serious heart failure and chest pain. Therefore, angioplasty is almost certain. Let us see when the doctors can conduct the angiography," he said.
Members of the Missionaries of Charity, the religious order the Roman Catholic nun founded in 1949, prayed for her recovery.
"We are having prayers all over the world for her recovery," said Sister Priscilla, the order's spokeswoman.
The charity, devoted to the poor, destitute and dying, has about 4,500 nuns in some 80 countries.
